title: What does a price cut really cost?
principle: A small price cut can need twice the sales. Can you get them?

screens.text: Let me start with a biscuit you know. In 1994, a small pack of Parle-G cost ₹4. In 2009, it still cost ₹4, even though its costs had kept rising. Before I tell you how, have a guess.

screens.prompt: Its costs kept going up, but the price stayed at ₹4. What do you think Parle did?

options.label: Took less profit on each pack
Made the pack a little lighter

screens.why: It made the pack lighter. In 2008, the pack went from 100 grams to 92.5 grams, and in 2009 to 88 grams. The price stayed at ₹4, so buyers kept buying.

screens.title: Tiny profit, huge sales
screens.text: Why not just raise the price? Parle did try once, around 2006. Sales fell sharply, and buyers wrote in to complain, so it quickly went back. Parle-G is very cheap, so it needs huge sales: about 40 crore biscuits a day by 2020.

screens.title: Price, cost and how many
screens.text: Parle's story shows how three numbers work together: price, cost, and how many you sell. This is called cost-volume-profit. Parle didn't dare raise its price. Small shops often make another mistake: they cut the price, and a small cut can take away much of what each sale leaves.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Parle keeps its price low and makes it work by selling crores of packets. Most small businesses can't sell that many. Imagine you run a chai stall near a bus stand. Your chai sells for ₹10. Milk, tea, sugar and the cup cost ₹6, so each cup leaves you ₹4.

screens.prompt: Your chai sells for ₹10 and costs ₹6. Cut the price to ₹8, which is 20% off. What happens to what each cup leaves you?
screens.why: Exactly. Each cup used to leave ₹4: ₹10 minus ₹6. At ₹8, it leaves ₹2. Your price fell by 20%, but what each cup leaves you fell by half.

wrong.a: That's what most people think. But the whole ₹2 comes out of the ₹4 left after costs. ₹8 − ₹6 leaves ₹2, which is half of ₹4.
wrong.c: ₹2 sounds small. But each cup only left you ₹4 before. Losing ₹2 of that ₹4 means each cup now leaves you half as much.

screens.prompt: Today, 300 cups a day leave you ₹4 each, so you keep ₹1,200. At ₹8, each cup leaves ₹2. How many cups keep ₹1,200?
screens.why: Right. ₹1,200 divided by ₹2 is 600 cups. Here, a 20% price cut means you must sell twice as many cups just to earn the same.

wrong.a: I see what you did: 20% off, so 20% more cups. But each cup now leaves half as much, so you need twice as many: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹2 = 600.
wrong.b: 450 is 50% more cups. But each cup now leaves half as much, so you need twice as many: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹2 = 600.

screens.prompt: At ₹8, you'd need 600 cups a day to earn the same. Even at full speed, your stall makes about 400. Can ₹8 work?

options.label: Yes. Cheaper chai brings more people
No. I can't make 600 cups a day
Yes, if people buy two cups each

screens.why: Right. You'd need 600 cups a day, and your stall makes 400. Before you cut a price, ask two things: will that many more people come, and can I make that much?

wrong.a: Some new people will come. But you'd need 600 cups a day, and your stall can only make 400.
wrong.c: Most people want one chai. And even if a few buy two, your stall can only make about 400 cups a day, not 600.

screens.prompt: Now the other way. You sell 300 cups and keep ₹1,200. At ₹12, each cup leaves ₹6. How many cups keep ₹1,200?
screens.why: Yes. ₹1,200 divided by ₹6 is 200 cups. You could lose 100 of your 300 buyers and still earn the same. But buyers may leave: Parle's buyers cared a lot about each rupee, so its price rise failed.

wrong.b: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹6 is 200, not 250. So you could lose 100 of your 300 buyers and still earn the same.
wrong.c: 300 is what you sell now. At ₹6 a cup, you need only ₹1,200 ÷ ₹6, which is 200 cups.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six businesses. Each wants to cut its price by 20%. For each one, tell me: could it really sell twice as much?

items.text: A barber with one chair, busy all day
A bakery with spare ovens, near a big new college
A tailor who already has more orders than he can sew
A water-can seller with an unused truck, in a growing colony
A chai stall on a quiet lane
A print shop with machines idle half the day, near many offices

screens.why: Right. A cut only works if you can sell much more: more buyers who'd come for a lower price, and room to make more for them. A busy barber has no room, and a quiet lane has few buyers.

screens.setup: One morning, the stall across the road drops its chai to ₹8. By evening, 50 of your 300 regulars have crossed the road. The other 250 stay, because they like your chai. You charge ₹10, and each cup costs ₹6.
screens.question: What do you do about your price?

options.label: Match him at ₹8
options.outcome: All 50 regulars come back, and you sell 300 cups again. But each cup now leaves ₹2, so you keep ₹600 a day instead of ₹1,200. You got the customers back but lost half your money.
options.why: To earn the same at ₹8, you'd need 600 cups a day. You only got back to 300. Matching a price cut can cost much more than losing a few customers.
options.better: Keep ₹10, and let those 50 go. Losing 50 cups costs you ₹200 a day; matching costs ₹600.

options.label: Keep ₹10, even if some leave
options.outcome: You sell 250 cups a day, and each still leaves ₹4. You keep ₹1,000 a day. Losing 50 customers cost you ₹200 a day, much less than a price cut would.
options.why: Well done. You did the sum before you reacted: 250 cups at ₹4 beats 300 cups at ₹2. The cut would have halved what every cup leaves you.

options.label: Cut to ₹9
options.outcome: At ₹9, 40 of the 50 come back, and you sell 290 cups. Each cup leaves ₹3, so you keep ₹870 a day. That's better than ₹600, but worse than staying at ₹10.
options.why: A smaller cut costs you less, but it still costs you. At ₹9, you'd need 400 cups a day to earn the same ₹1,200.
options.better: Keep ₹10. 250 cups at ₹4 leaves ₹1,000, more than 290 cups at ₹3.

screens.text: The 20% price cut took ___ of what each cup left you, so you needed ___ cups to earn the same.
screens.why: Right. At ₹10, each cup left ₹4; at ₹8, only ₹2. The less each sale leaves you, the more a small cut costs you. Before you cut a price, work out how many more you must sell, and ask if you really can.

summary: Price, cost and how many you sell work together. This is cost-volume-profit.
When each sale leaves you little, a small price cut can halve it, so you may need twice the sales.
Before you cut a price, check if you can really sell that many more.

cards.front: Price ₹50, cost ₹40. You cut the price to ₹45. How much less does each sale leave?
cards.back: ₹50 − ₹40 = ₹10. ₹45 − ₹40 = ₹5. The price fell 10%, but what each sale leaves fell by half.

cards.front: You sell 100 a day, keeping ₹4 each. A cut leaves ₹2 each. How many sales keep the same money?
cards.back: ₹400 ÷ ₹2 = 200. Twice the sales, just to earn the same.

cards.front: A rival cuts prices and you lose 1 in 6 customers. Matching would halve what each sale leaves. What's usually safer?
cards.back: Losing 1 in 6 sales costs less than halving every sale.

sources.label: Parle-G clocks best sales in 8 decades (Business Today, 9 Jun 2020)
